item.title: The Brand Age, Paul Graham
item.description:
Paul Graham is the co-founder of Y Combinator and one of the foremost philosophers of the Computer Science world. For 25 years he has been publishing thoughtful essays on his blog — though rarely: in 2025, for instance, he published just four pieces. In March 2026 a new one appeared — «The Brand Age». I’d like to discuss it.

Why does this matter to me? Among the authors I follow, Paul Graham sits at the top. I’ve referenced his essays several times before — in my roundup of resources for product managers, in «The 10 Deadly Sins of a Product Manager», and in «Thinking Through Writing». I’m also drawn to his style: clarifying footnotes and acknowledgments to well-known specialists who review his drafts. In this latest essay, for example, Sam Altman is among the reviewers. And an equally important factor — no ads, no promotion of any services.

item.title: Product Strategy ≠ Template
item.description:
The goal of strategy is to move away from «build whatever anyone asks for» toward a deliberate position aimed at creating a better future for both users and the business.

As tempting as it would be, there is no universal product strategy template — no template at all, really. The format depends on the maturity of the company and its people, team structure, business model, business strategy, and a whole host of other factors.

item.title: Second Brain: PARA × Obsidian × Granola × Claude
item.description:
A few years ago I was organizing notes using the Zettelkasten method in VS Code. A lot has changed since then — largely due to the exponential growth of LLMs and agentic AI. I want to share my current tool stack, which helps reduce cognitive load and keep information from slipping through the cracks when time is scarce: PARA × Obsidian × Granola × Claude.

The article is called «Second Brain» — which means we’re building a system that mirrors the structure of the human brain.

item.title: People Who Write Interestingly
item.description:
I want to share a list of people on the internet who write interesting content on product-adjacent topics and are worth following. I often return to articles from these authors — especially when I’m looking for creative inspiration.

  • Marty Cagan — an iconic figure in the product world and author of a popular series of books: Inspired, Empowered, and Transformed. Founder of SVPG and an active blogger on product management. His ideas about product discovery and empowered teams have become industry standards.
  • Paul Graham — co-founder of Y Combinator and author of wonderful essays that remain relevant across time. He writes about startups, thinking, and decision-making — concisely, precisely, and without fluff.
  • Andrew Chen — partner at Andreessen Horowitz and author of a popular blog on growth marketing.
  • Vitalik Buterin — founder of Ethereum and a prolific blogger. He writes deep technical and philosophical essays on decentralization and the future of technology.
  • Grigory Bakunov — founder of radio-t, former Director of Technology Dissemination at Yandex. Writes about technology, management, and life in tech — sharply and without corporate-speak.
  • Oleg Yakubenkov — founder of GoPractice and author of the most popular product analytics blog in the Russian-speaking market. His simulators and articles are must-reads for anyone looking to get a handle on metrics and unit economics.
  • Artem Gorbunov & Co. — a collection of practical advice on product topics from cult-status specialists. Short and to the point — covering writing, interfaces, negotiations, and management.
  • Melissa Perri — author of Escaping the Build Trap. She writes about product as a value system, product culture, and why companies get stuck in feature factory mode.
  • Teresa Torres — author of Continuous Discovery Habits. Her blog covers discovery practices: opportunity solution trees, customer interviews, and the habits of strong product teams.
  • Wes Kao — runs an excellent applied blog on management, product thinking, and career development. Publishes regularly.
  • Ben Thompson — technology analyst and author of the Stratechery blog. He takes a deep dive into the business strategies of tech companies, platform models, and competitive market dynamics.
  • Valeria Rozova — product leader and curator of an article library on product topics written by graduates of her courses. The articles are highly practical and detailed — a great resource for developing specific product skills.

item.title: Prioritization Methods: ICE, RICE, DRICE
item.description: Ein, zwei, drei… There are endless ways to prioritize tasks. Every product I’ve ever worked on had its own original ranking method, each with its own quirks. For a quick tour of the approaches used at large companies, check out Misha Karpov’s talk at a Yandex product meetup [1]. As for my personal favorites — there’s the energy method, where priorities are chosen based on how you’re feeling, and the intuitive method, where you simply listen to your gut. The only problem is that teams rarely agree to follow either approach.

item.title: 10 Deadly Sins of a Beginning Product Manager
item.description:
This article was originally published on habr.com.

These «deadly sins» can serve as a self-assessment checklist for both beginner and more experienced managers.

So, here are the mistakes — and how to fix them.

1. Believing in multitasking

Every product manager faces enormous flows of information, including all manner of product development initiatives and ideas that no single person can possibly process within the time available. Stakeholders push their agendas, users complain, the calendar is packed with meetings, and the Product Backlog grows day by day.

item.title: Thinking Through Writing
item.description:
I came across a fascinating interview with Andrei Styskin (Director at Amazon, former CEO of the search division at Yandex), in which Andrei talks about some interesting aspects of Amazon’s internal culture — specifically, the «document-centric» approach to meetings and decision-making.

  1. Every meeting is a collaborative effort in which participants work together on a pre-prepared document focused on a specific problem. Part of the time (10 to 20 minutes) is spent reading the document independently; the rest is used for discussion and commentary. If open questions remain after the meeting, another meeting is scheduled in the same format. The process continues until the requirements are unambiguously defined and agreed upon by all stakeholders.
  2. Requirements for any product or feature are developed using the «Working Backwards» method, through writing two documents: a «Press Release» and a «FAQ.» The product manager writes a press release long before the release date, thereby forming a vision of the ideal launch outcome — a north star that the product team can orient toward throughout development.
  3. All decisions are made through document reviews, not through informal verbal conversations in meetings or by the coffee machine, as so often happens in most workplaces.

Reflecting on my time at Yandex (a great company, though not quite global in scale — for comparison, in 2024 Yandex’s market cap was $10 billion, while Amazon’s was $2 trillion), I can say that the company’s internal culture encourages employees to express their thinking in writing: at Yandex, it’s standard practice to maintain detailed wiki documentation, write thorough task descriptions in the issue tracker, discuss questions in comments, and keep internal blogs — both public and anonymous. The more senior an employee’s position, the more persuasively and concisely they tend to write and communicate their ideas.

item.title: Books and Materials for Product Managers
item.description:
There’s no shortage of materials online for developing product skills and broadening your horizons. But I want to gather only the most useful, practical, and valuable ones here. This list is constantly evolving: new materials are added, outdated ones are removed. I hope you find something worth your time.

Introduction to Product Culture and the Profession

  • Essay «How to Do Great Work,» Paul Graham. An essay by the iconic Paul Graham on how to do your work well — full of advice and reflection. Recommended reading for everyone starting out in their career, not just product managers.
  • Article «Good Product Manager / Bad Product Manager,» Ben Horowitz. A short article written in 2012 that remains just as relevant today. It gives a clear sense of what qualities a good product manager should have.
  • Article «Amazon Leadership Principles,» Amazon. Amazon’s 14 leadership principles — what the company expects from its managers, and what interviewers will probe during Amazon interview loops. If they don’t resonate on first read, it’s worth coming back to them later.

Managing Yourself and Your Teams

  • «Getting Things Done,» David Allen
  • «Jedi Techniques,» Maxim Dorofeev
  • «Herding Cats,» J. Hank Rainwater
  • «Managing Humans,» Michael Lopp

Research

  • «The Mom Test,» Rob Fitzpatrick. An essential classic on preparing for user interviews. The approach has its fans and its critics alike — but everyone has read it, and no one has been left indifferent.
  • «Running Lean: Iterate from Plan A to a Plan That Works,» Ash Maurya
  • Video «How to Talk to Users,» Eric Migicovsky (Y Combinator)
  • Video «ABCDX Segmentation,» Artem Azevich (IIDF Accelerator)
  • Video «Market Sizing,» Alexander Skurikhin (IIDF Accelerator, Yandex)
  • producthunt.com

Analytics

  • «Playing with Numbers: How Analytics Helps Video Games Thrive,» Vasily Sabirov. Probably the only book on product analytics written by a Russian author. It reads less like a textbook and more like a conversation with a product analyst.
  • «Say It with Charts,» Gene Zelazny
  • GoPractice Blog. Simply an encyclopedia of product analytics and product management knowledge. The articles are exceptionally well written. Best read slowly and carefully — evening tea in hand.
  • Free course «Fundamentals of Statistics and A/B Testing» by Yandex Practicum. An excellent introductory course on statistics and A/B testing, built by a team of mathematicians at Practicum.
  • Free course «Fundamentals of Statistics» by Anatoly Karpov. The most popular statistics course in the Russian-speaking web — Anatoly breaks down both descriptive and inferential statistics in a clear, structured way. It has become a classic in the Runet.

Strategy

  • «Good Strategy Bad Strategy,» Richard Rumelt. A foundational conceptual book on strategy. It explains what good strategy looks like — and what bad strategy looks like (which is most of what passes for strategy). There’s a short summary on my blog.
  • «The Goal: A Process of Ongoing Improvement,» Eliyahu Goldratt

Delivery Management / Backlog Management

  • «Getting Real: The Smarter, Faster, Easier Way to Build a Successful Web Application,» Jason Fried + David Heinemeier Hansson + Matthew Linderman
  • Article «20 Product Prioritization Techniques: A Map and Guided Tour». A detailed breakdown of 20 techniques for prioritizing your backlog or hypotheses.
  • Article «RICE: Simple prioritization for product managers,» Intercom. The original article from Intercom, where this prioritization method was born. It also includes an XLS template you can use right out of the box.

Interviews and Hiring

  • «The Art of Recruiting: How to Evaluate a Person in One Hour,» Svetlana Ivanova
  • «Who: The A Method for Hiring,» Geoff Smart and Randy Street
  • «Cracking the PM Interview: How to Land a Product Manager Job in Technology,» Gayle Laakmann McDowell
  • «Decode and Conquer,» Lewis C. Lin. One of Lewis Lin’s books — though if you can, it’s worth reading his others as well.
  • Podcast «Sobes» (Interview)
  • Podcast «Dva Stula» (Two Chairs)

Computer Science Fundamentals

  • Free Python courses «Python Generation». A series of free Python courses for absolute beginners by professional developer and educator Timur Guev. Timur comes from a generation of mathematicians who scored 100 on the national math exam and a generation of engineers who went on to work at FAANG companies. You won’t find better beginner courses than this series.
  • Free SQL practice platform sql-ex.ru. One of the best — if not the best — SQL practice platforms, and it’s free. It features a huge number of exercises. I recommend working through them to solidify your SQL query-writing skills. Don’t let the outdated interface put you off.
  • «System Design Interview,» Alex Xu

Data Science Fundamentals

  • Article «Machine Learning for People,» vas3k. A comprehensive introduction for anyone who finally wants to make sense of machine learning — in plain language, without formulas or theorems, with real-world problem examples and their solutions.
  • «Machine Learning for Humans,» Vishal Maini, Samir Sabri

Inspiring Stories

  • «Elon Musk: Tesla, SpaceX, and the Quest for a Fantastic Future,» Ashlee Vance. The story of Musk’s development as a businessman — the obstacles he overcame, the risks he took. Including a trip to Russia in 2001 to try to buy an intercontinental ballistic missile.
  • «Pour Your Heart Into It: How Starbucks Built a Company One Cup at a Time,» Dori Jones Yang, Howard Schultz
  • «The Yandex Book,» Dmitry Sokolov-Mitrich. The story of Yandex’s rise — from its origins to its IPO. About the personalities of its founders. About how Sergey Brin and Larry Page came to Moscow in 2003 to acquire the company, but Arkady Volozh and Ilya Segalovich turned them down — and went on to build Russia’s most innovative tech company.

item.title: The Evolution of Goal-Setting Frameworks: From OKR to NCT
item.description:
I came across an interesting approach to goal-setting — NCT (Narratives, Commitments, Tasks) by Ravi Mehta [1]. What makes it compelling is that it positions itself as an alternative to OKR and could be genuinely useful for many product teams. Before diving into NCT, let’s take a quick look at the history of goal-setting frameworks.

In 1954, Peter Drucker introduced the concept of MBO (Management by Objectives) in his book The Practice of Management [2]. The core idea is to set goals at the company level and cascade them down to individual contributors at every level. For example, many services within Yandex still use a similar approach today — there’s even a dedicated internal tool for cascading goals called «Golzyatnitsa.»

item.title: Product CEO: How a Product Manager Creates Meaning and Communicates Value
item.description:
This article was originally published on Delovoy Mir.

Technology today is advancing at a breakneck pace. There’s even a concept called «technological singularity» — the idea that in some hypothetical future, explosive technological growth will fundamentally transform our civilization.

But it’s worth remembering that technology doesn’t enter our lives on its own. It arrives through IT products — products built to solve specific problems or meet the particular needs of their audiences.

item.title: Tools and Services for Product Managers
item.description:
I want to share the services and tools I regularly use to get work done. Maybe you’ll discover something new and make your workday a little more comfortable.

Product Awareness and UX

  • ProductHunt — the go-to resource for developing a broad product sense. It helps you stay on top of new product launches and the evolution of existing ones.
  • UserOnboard — a library of detailed UX teardowns of popular services like Gmail, Instagram, Apple Music, Netflix, and more.

Research and A/B Testing

  • Statista — a knowledge base with up-to-date market analytics and research. A corporate account with access to detailed reports is great, but the free version still lets you browse basic reports.
  • Yandex Wordstat — useful for analyzing user search queries in the Russian-language internet segment.
  • ResearchGate — a vast library of academic papers on virtually any topic.
  • Evan’s Awesome A/B Tools — one of the oldest and most popular online tools for planning and analyzing A/B tests: sample size estimation and experiment result evaluation.
  • GoodUI — a pattern library featuring A/B tests and breakdowns of their results.

Diagrams, Flowcharts, and Graphics

  • Miro — the de facto standard for visual collaboration.
  • Mermaid — a tool for generating diagrams from text descriptions (code). Integrates with many modern wiki systems: Notion, Google Docs, Confluence.
  • Draw.io — a simple and convenient tool for creating more complex diagrams and flowcharts than Mermaid supports. Lets you save source files to Google Drive and requires no registration or login.
  • Canva — the best tool for creating graphic assets. The free version is more than enough for most everyday tasks.
  • Emojipedia — an emoji reference for adding a touch of personality to requirements docs and task descriptions.

Personal and Team Productivity

  • Things — a clean and beautifully designed to-do app for Mac and iOS, perfect for design perfectionists who appreciate minimalism and good typography.
  • Ilya Birman’s Typography Layout — a keyboard layout for writing polished text and typing the right symbols quickly (✓≈≠₽x↓−""). If you write a lot and care about how your text looks, give Birman’s layout a try — it’s a joy to use.
  • Obsidian — an app for organizing notes in Markdown (.md) format.
  • ChatGPT — a replacement for Google search.
  • Google Sheets, Slides, Colab — the bare essentials for any product manager.

Rapid MVP Development and Vibe Coding

  • Cursor IDE — a code editor on steroids that lets you build apps and services with minimal programming knowledge, and do it fast.
  • GitHub / GitHub Pages — deploy static sites to production quickly and for free.
  • Vercel — deploy more complex services to production quickly and for free.

item.title: The Growth Dilemma of Educational Course Economics
item.description:
While comparing the top edTech companies in the Russian-speaking internet market, I noticed a funny scaling problem baked into their course economics — one they’ve all learned to live with. I’m not talking about product-driven edTech platforms like Lingualeo, but companies that create educational courses for upskilling or career transitions.

Product EdTech Theorem #1

The absence of deadlines in an educational course leads to ↑ Revenue and ↓ Completion Rate (COR). Conversely, having deadlines leads to ↓ Revenue and ↑ Completion Rate.

item.title: Product Management Is Marketing Management
item.description:
And a product manager is a marketing specialist.

This definition is obvious to people who studied marketing in college. But it’s not always clear to those who came to product management from a technical background.

As someone who came up through the technical ranks, I long believed that «marketing» was limited to finding promotion channels, communicating a product’s value to users, and selling goods (physical or digital — didn’t matter). But that understanding of marketing is very, very far from the truth.

item.title: Loyalty ≠ Satisfaction
item.description:
Loyalty

Customer Loyalty is a user’s devotion to a brand or product. It means that, all else being equal, a user will choose our product over the alternatives. This choice is often emotional — a user who loves a product will recommend it to friends and family.

The standard metric for measuring customer loyalty is the NPS (Net Promoter Score), whose growth is positively correlated with sales growth and market share gains. This relationship, combined with the simplicity of measuring the index, is what made it so widely adopted. That said, NPS has its fair share of pitfalls — here’s a good article on the subject: «12 подводных камней Net Promoter Score».

item.title: On Leadership
item.description:
The original interview was published on VC.


— Konstantin, why do you think being a leader is worthwhile or interesting?

— Let’s start with what leadership actually is. There are many different definitions. Peter Drucker, for instance, wrote: «Leadership is the ability to help a person go beyond their own limitations.»

Leadership is the skill of positively influencing people — one that allows you to achieve ambitious goals through the efforts of every member of a group.

item.title: Calculating Classic, Rolling, and Full Retention in Python
item.description: In this post, I want to walk through how to manually calculate 3 types of Retention metrics using Python and Pandas, and how to plot a Retention curve using Matplotlib. Most of the time, a product manager will use an analytics platform to analyze data and metrics — but let’s imagine our PM is stranded on a desert island with nothing but a Python interpreter and a few extra libraries. That’s exactly what we’ll use.

item.title: Chart Templates for Data Visualization
item.description:
Product managers present constantly: they run research → share findings; a new quarter kicks off → they announce goals; a quarter, half-year, or year wraps up → they review results; and so on.

Data visualization tends to be a weak spot in these presentations, so I decided to put together a Google Sheets template where I’ll collect and update reference chart examples covering the most common product, business, and financial data scenarios.

item.title: The Zettelkasten Note-Taking Method
item.description:
Zettelkasten is an increasingly popular method for organizing notes and ideas, developed by the extraordinarily prolific German sociologist Niklas Luhmann, who over the course of his life managed to write more than 70 major academic books and 500 scholarly articles, and received prestigious doctoral honors and awards for his contributions to sociology.

The Zettelkasten note-taking method helped Luhmann acquire knowledge more effectively and engage in deep research. This gives rise to a hypothesis: «If Zettelkasten helped Luhmann absorb new knowledge, it can help us too.» All that remains is to put this promising hypothesis to the test.

On English- and Russian-language resources, Zettelkasten only started gaining attention in 2020, following the publication of David Clear’s article «Zettelkasten — How One German Scholar Was So Freakishly Productive,» which has also been translated into Russian on Habr. This is all the more surprising given that Luhmann never made a secret of his unique knowledge management method — a detailed description in the original can be found in German academic journals from 1981–1987 (originals in German).

item.title: How to Run a Retrospective for a Large Team
item.description:
A retrospective is a form of group reflection — a tool for continuous improvement and cultural change within a team.

Most of us encounter the term «retro» in the context of end-of-sprint ceremonies in iterative development. However, the majority of teams don’t follow Scrum or any iterative approach to building IT products. That’s no reason to abandon either self-reflection or group reflection when hitting key project milestones.

Below is a detailed 8-step plan with timings for running an engaging retrospective with a large team (10+ people).

item.title: A/B Test Design Template
item.description:
A Google Sheets template for designing A/B tests. It helps you structure an experiment before launch — from writing the hypothesis to calculating how long the test should run.

Download template

What’s inside

Experiment description — a hypothesis written in the following format: «If [product change], then [target metric] will change by [expected result], because [research data].» This section also includes the target metric and the experiment start date.

item.title: ICE, RICE, DRICE Prioritization Framework Template
item.description:
A Google Sheets template for prioritizing product initiatives using three frameworks: ICE, RICE, and DRICE. For a deeper dive into the methods, see «ICE, RICE, DRICE Prioritization Methods».

Download template

What’s inside

ICE — the simplest prioritization method. Each initiative is scored on three dimensions from 0 to 10:

  • Impact (effect on the metric)
  • Confidence (certainty in the estimate)
  • Ease (ease of implementation)
  • ICE Score = I × C × E

item.title: On the Certified Scrum Product Owner Certification
item.description:
In his book Empowered: Ordinary People, Extraordinary Products, Marty Cagan recommends that aspiring product managers get CSPO-certified early in their careers. I want to share what you can actually expect from this training and certification — beyond just another achievement to add to your profile (and a fairly pricey one at that).

The training runs for two full days. The first day covers agile and scrum fundamentals through group exercises, with a brief overview of other product development methodologies. For anyone just entering the profession, this day is genuinely valuable — it builds a deeper, more intentional understanding of scrum. That knowledge serves as a useful baseline for evaluating and comparing the processes at your own company or within your product.

More experienced product managers will find the first day helpful for formalizing and structuring what they already know. Most of us work directly with development teams, and a fresh perspective can bring new energy and creative thinking to those relationships.
